title: Design Underground System
description:
# Design Underground System

An underground railway system records when passengers check in and check out. It must answer the average travel time for every directed route from one station to another.

Implement the `UndergroundSystem` class:

* `UndergroundSystem()` initializes the system.
* `void checkIn(int id, String stationName, int t)` records that passenger `id` enters `stationName` at time `t`. A passenger is never checked in twice at the same time.
* `void checkOut(int id, String stationName, int t)` records that passenger `id` leaves at `stationName` at time `t`, completing one direct trip from the passenger's last check-in station to this checkout station.
* `double getAverageTime(String startStation, String endStation)` returns the average duration of all completed direct trips from `startStation` to `endStation`. The reverse direction is a different route. Active trips that have not checked out yet are not part of any average.

All method calls are consistent: a checked-out passenger has a previous unmatched check-in, query routes have at least one completed trip, and each passenger's checkout time is greater than that passenger's check-in time. Events are given in chronological order.

In operation examples, the first array lists operations and the second lists their argument lists, paired by index and executed left to right. The first operation constructs the object; later operations use that same object. Outputs align by index too: constructors and void methods produce `null`; an empty argument list `[]` means no arguments.

## Example 1

**Input:**
["UndergroundSystem","checkIn","checkIn","checkIn","checkOut","checkOut","checkOut","getAverageTime","getAverageTime","checkIn","getAverageTime","checkOut","getAverageTime"]
[[],[45,"Leyton",3],[32,"Paradise",8],[27,"Leyton",10],[45,"Waterloo",15],[27,"Waterloo",20],[32,"Cambridge",22],["Paradise","Cambridge"],["Leyton","Waterloo"],[10,"Leyton",24],["Leyton","Waterloo"],[10,"Waterloo",38],["Leyton","Waterloo"]]

**Output:**
[null,null,null,null,null,null,null,14.00000,11.00000,null,11.00000,null,12.00000]

## Constraints

* `1 <= id, t <= 10^6`
* `1 <= stationName.length, startStation.length, endStation.length <= 10`
* Station names contain only uppercase letters, lowercase letters, and digits.
* There will be at most `2 * 10^4` total calls.
* Answers within `10^-5` of the actual value are accepted.

tests.description: Averages are kept per start-end pair and update after each checkout.
Route keys must not collide when station-name boundaries differ.
The same passenger id can be reused after checkout and should create a new trip.
An active trip must not affect the route average until it checks out.
Station names are case-sensitive and may contain digits.
Many overlapping trips on one route require a non-overflowing aggregate.

solutions.name: RouteKey Object Aggregate
solutions.description:
## Approach

Store each active passenger trip by card id, and store completed route statistics in a hash map keyed by a RouteKey value object containing start and end station. Each checkout removes the active trip, builds the route key, and adds the duration to the route aggregate.

## Key Insight

A route is a pair, not a concatenated word. Giving the pair its own equality and hash code avoids key collisions such as A->BC versus AB->C while keeping average queries constant time.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(1) average for checkIn, checkOut, and getAverageTime
- Space Complexity: O(P + R), where P is the number of active passengers and R is the number of completed routes

solutions.name: Nested Route Maps
solutions.description:
## Approach

Keep active check-ins in one map. For completed routes, use a first map from start station to a second map from end station to the aggregate total time and count. Checkout updates exactly one nested cell.

## Key Insight

Nested maps preserve the two-dimensional route structure directly. The start and end station never have to be packed into a string, so direction and station boundaries stay explicit.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(1) average per operation
- Space Complexity: O(P + R), where active passengers and distinct routes dominate storage

solutions.name: Delimited String Route Key
solutions.description:
## Approach

Represent an active check-in as a small object and represent a completed route with a string key containing a separator that cannot appear in station names. The aggregate value is a long array holding total duration and trip count.

## Key Insight

The prompt restricts station names to letters and digits, so a non-alphanumeric separator makes string keys safe. This keeps the implementation compact while still avoiding ambiguous concatenation.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(1) average for each operation
- Space Complexity: O(P + R) for active trips and route aggregates

solutions.name: Station Id Compression
solutions.description:
## Approach

Assign each station a compact integer id the first time it appears. Active trips store the start id and check-in time, while route statistics are stored by a packed long containing the start id and end id.

## Key Insight

Once station names become ids, the route pair can be encoded without allocating a new string for every checkout or query. The long key still preserves direction and pair boundaries exactly.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(1) average per operation
- Space Complexity: O(P + S + R), including station ids, active trips, and route aggregates

solutions.name: Online Running Average
solutions.description:
## Approach

Store active trips by passenger id. For each route, store only the current average and the count of completed trips, then update the average incrementally whenever another trip finishes.

## Key Insight

The query asks for an average, not the raw list of durations. Updating the average online avoids large integer totals while still returning the exact running mean within the required floating-point tolerance.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(1) average for all operations
- Space Complexity: O(P + R), because each active passenger and each completed route stores constant data
